anglicanism.1: Present in some evangelical outreach, such as Alpha courses, and absent from most parishes.
anglicanism.2: Published school admissions criteria can favor worshipping families.
anglicanism.6: Survivors being told processes were followed when they were not is not recorded.
anglicanism.17: IICSA found survivors' accounts were disbelieved in documented cases.
anglicanism.21: Survivors' repeated complaints failed (IICSA), but helplessness is not an inquiry finding.
anglicanism.22: Oversight of clergy lives runs through the bishop's licence and the tied house.

christianity.1: A grieving visitor is told, "God brought you here" and "You're home now."
christianity.2: After a church helps, a questioner hears, "After everything this church has done for you."
christianity.3: Heaven is presented as the ultimate deferred reward: no more tears, reunion, eternal joy.
christianity.4: After you stop attending, texts ask, "We miss you" and "Is everything okay spiritually?"
christianity.5: Christianity often begins by telling the person they are a sinner before God.
christianity.6: A person says, "This church hurt me," and is told, "Don't let bitterness take root."
christianity.7: Members must test everything against Scripture, but a different conclusion proves them wrong.
christianity.8: Worship is engineered for peaks, and dry Sundays are framed as your hidden sin.
christianity.9: "Just accept Jesus" becomes baptism, membership, tithing, serving and submission.
christianity.10: "God's will" is kept vague enough to justify almost anything, even forgiving abuse.
christianity.11: Churches accuse wounded members of being "divisive" after leadership created the division.
christianity.12: A survivor reports abuse, and the church says it did not happen, then calls them bitter.
christianity.13: A believer is trained to accept weekly self-denigration until it sounds like worship.
christianity.14: Christianity can isolate through warnings against "the world" and "bad company".
christianity.15: Questioners are sent to elders and mentors who all say: submit, forgive, stay.
christianity.16: Small-group leaders and "concerned friends" text instead of the pastor confronting the critic.
christianity.17: A church labels a critic bitter, divisive, rebellious, or under demonic attack.
christianity.18: Leaders say they are "looking into it," then weeks or months pass with no update.
christianity.19: A teenager "chooses" baptism after years of hell teaching and fear of being unsaved.
christianity.20: The church teaches you are sinful, then offers forgiveness and "the peace of God."
christianity.21: A member with hard questions is told to pray, submit, wait and stop doubting.
christianity.22: Leaders tell members not to date unbelievers or listen to critics, to "guard their hearts."
christianity.23: Adult believers are called sheep who need shepherds, or children who need spiritual fathers.
christianity.24: The believer's identity is replaced with categories: sinner, saved, servant, sheep.
christianity.25: Abuse is bypassed with "forgive seventy times seven" or "vengeance is the Lord's."
christianity.26: Churches may pressure members to tithe, give offerings, and volunteer endless unpaid labor.
christianity.27: Churches may manufacture crisis through hell, demons, spiritual warfare and end-times prophecy.
christianity.28: A church that called someone "family" quietly stops inviting them after they question it.
christianity.29: A volunteer leaves after burnout; the church recruits another and calls it "God providing."
christianity.30: A pastor never says "Shun her," but preaches about wolves and divisive people.

hare-krishna.1: Newcomers are drawn in by chanting, prasadam, music and the promise of joyful devotion.
hare-krishna.2: ISKCON often offers prasadam, chanting, festivals, music and a joyful devotional atmosphere.
hare-krishna.3: ISKCON future-fakes through return to Godhead, liberation, and eternal service to Krishna.
hare-krishna.4: Someone leaving ISKCON may be pulled back through prasadam, kirtan and devotee friendships.
hare-krishna.5: ISKCON can devalue ordinary identity by calling material life illusion, or maya.
hare-krishna.7: Reluctance to serve Krishna is called maya, so its absence is diagnosed and corrected.
hare-krishna.8: Some nights kirtan lifts the room and some nights it doesn't; Krishna's choosing explains both.
hare-krishna.9: A newcomer who enjoys prasadam must then chant rounds, follow principles, serve and surrender.
hare-krishna.10: Guru authority is devotion when attractive and individual imperfection when abuse is exposed.
hare-krishna.11: ISKCON communities may accuse leavers of being captured by maya.
hare-krishna.12: A devotee reports abuse, and the response may deny it or call it isolated imperfection.
hare-krishna.13: Newcomers are slowly normalized into the temple schedule, regulated diet and guru devotion.
hare-krishna.14: ISKCON can isolate through temple life and warnings against materialistic association.
hare-krishna.15: ISKCON triangulates through guru, temple president, senior devotees and fear of maya.
hare-krishna.16: A questioning devotee may be approached by senior devotees, temple leaders and friends.
hare-krishna.17: Former devotees may be labeled fallen, offensive, in maya, or lacking surrender.
hare-krishna.18: A devotee who questions guru authority is told to chant more and avoid offenses.
hare-krishna.19: Newcomers "choose" devotional life after immersion in chanting, prasadam and community warmth.
hare-krishna.20: ISKCON can bond through sweetness and shame, paired with devaluation of material life.
hare-krishna.21: A burned-out devotee is told to chant more, serve more purely, and surrender.
hare-krishna.22: Guru obedience, temple service and diet are framed as loving purification.
hare-krishna.23: Devotees may be treated as fallen if they desire ordinary family, romance or autonomy.
hare-krishna.24: Devotee identity replaces ordinary identity: servant of Krishna, follower of guru.
hare-krishna.26: ISKCON financial control may appear through donations, book distribution and temple labor.
hare-krishna.27: ISKCON may manufacture crisis around maya, bad association and leaving devotional service.
hare-krishna.28: A devotee who leaves may be described as fallen, in maya, or lacking surrender.
hare-krishna.29: A devotee who leaves is replaced by a newcomer drawn by kirtan and prasadam.
hare-krishna.30: ISKCON can say temple life is voluntary while outside life is called maya.

jainism.1: A seeker is drawn by radical nonviolence, discipline, simplicity and the seriousness of ahimsa.
jainism.2: Jain communities may offer support through food, business networks, family and temple life.
jainism.3: Jainism offers liberation from karma, escape from rebirth and release through discipline.
jainism.4: A Jain leaving strict practice may be told they are accumulating karma or abandoning ahimsa.
jainism.5: Jainism can devalue through impossible purity, since ordinary life constantly causes harm.
jainism.6: Someone says fasting expectations are harming them and hears, "You are attached to the body."
jainism.7: Forceful naming of a teacher's harm is himsa, and gentle naming is ignored.
jainism.8: An eight-day fast is honored one Paryushana and unnoticed the next, so vows escalate.
jainism.9: A Jain's vegetarianism is followed by stricter rules: fasting, festival vows, purity rules.
jainism.10: Dietary rules may be framed as discipline, family expectation or purity, by audience.
jainism.11: Jain communities may accuse people of violence for relaxing dietary rules.
jainism.12: A person says fasting pressure harmed them; the response may deny harm.
jainism.13: Dietary restriction can escalate from vegetarianism to fasting, vows and shame around eating.
jainism.14: Jain isolation can happen through strict dietary rules, fasting culture and family honor.
jainism.15: Jain triangulation works through family, temple community, monks, nuns and moral comparison.
jainism.16: A Jain who loosens dietary restrictions may be pressured by parents, relatives and monks.
jainism.17: A person who stops fasting may be smeared as indulgent, violent, impure, or lazy.
jainism.18: A person says food shame is harming them and is told they are attached to the body.
jainism.19: A person "chooses" strict diet when ordinary eating feels morally contaminated.
jainism.20: Jain practice can create cycles of purity anxiety and relief.
jainism.21: A person who tries to stop fasting is told they are attached, impure, or karmically careless.
jainism.23: Adults may be corrected like children over food, fasting, purity and temple attendance.
jainism.24: The person may become defined by purity, restraint, diet, fasting and karma reduction.
jainism.26: Jain financial control may appear through temple donations and festival sponsorships.
jainism.27: Jain communities may manufacture crisis around food, fasting, purity and karma.
jainism.28: Someone who relaxes dietary rules may be treated as indulgent, careless or spiritually weak.
jainism.30: Strict food rules and fasting are called voluntary, but shame makes refusal morally costly.

new-age.1: Seekers are welcomed with healing, vibration, soul family and "you were meant to be here."
new-age.2: New Age spaces may offer free circles, astrology readings and "soul family" belonging.
new-age.3: New Age systems future-fake through awakening, ascension, abundance and starseed destiny.
new-age.4: Someone leaving a New Age circle may be told they are blocked or resisting abundance.
new-age.5: New Age movements can devalue through softer language: blocked, low vibration, unhealed.
new-age.6: Someone questions a teacher's prices and is told they are in scarcity mindset.
new-age.7: Seekers are told to trust intuition, until it says leave, and then it is fear or ego.
new-age.8: Manifestation hits prove the method, misses prove your vibration, and courses fill the gap.
new-age.9: A person buys a healing session, then needs a package, retreat, mastermind or certification.
new-age.10: "Energy" can explain attraction, illness, money and abuse without ever being testable.
new-age.11: A coach may accuse a client of scarcity mindset for questioning prices.
new-age.12: A client questions a healer, and the teacher says they are triggered, projecting or blocked.
new-age.13: People become normalized into paying for sessions, retreats, masterminds and certifications.
new-age.14: New Age groups isolate through "soul family" and claims that outsiders are low vibration.
new-age.15: New Age triangulation runs through guides, astrology charts, soul contracts and "the universe."
new-age.16: A person leaving a healer may be told, "You're in resistance," "Your ego is scared."
new-age.17: Former clients may be labeled low vibration, narcissistic, unhealed, or scarcity-minded.
new-age.18: A client asking about money or harm gets vague answers about energy and alignment.
new-age.19: A client "chooses" costly sessions after being told their abundance block needs the next one.
new-age.20: A teacher says the client is blocked, then offers paid healing or retreats as relief.
new-age.21: A client who fails to manifest is told they have deeper blocks or low vibration.
new-age.22: Teachers control clients through language of healing, alignment and soul purpose.
new-age.23: Teachers call clients unhealed, blocked, low vibration, or not ready.
new-age.24: The person is rebranded as empath, starseed, healer, lightworker or abundance channel.
new-age.26: New Age financial control may appear through retreats, coaching packages and certifications.
new-age.27: New Age leaders may manufacture crisis through ascension windows and twin flame deadlines.
new-age.28: A client who stops paying or leaves may be labeled low vibration, unhealed, or fear-based.
new-age.30: A coach says clients freely choose programs, while hesitation is diagnosed as scarcity.

plymouth-brethren.6: The church says it does not prevent contact with families, and testimony says otherwise.
plymouth-brethren.9: Technology rules changed from prohibition to approved systems, according to former members.
plymouth-brethren.12: A member was interrogated over an alleged hack as leaders protected "the Lord's interest".
plymouth-brethren.17: Former members are investigated and pressured; the ABC reported private investigators.
plymouth-brethren.20: Belonging and fear of withdrawal alternate.
plymouth-brethren.21: Every door leads to the same network.
plymouth-brethren.23: Adults' friendships are governed by separation, and technology and education are managed.
plymouth-brethren.29: Family life continues without the withdrawn.

shia-islam.1: A seeker may be drawn in through hospitality, majlis, Karbala narratives and mourning rituals.
shia-islam.2: Shia communities may welcome seekers through majlis gatherings, mourning rituals and meals.
shia-islam.3: Shia Islam offers a future of loyalty, martyrdom, justice and vindication of the oppressed.
shia-islam.4: A person drifting away may be pulled back through mourning, majlis and loyalty to Imam Husayn.
shia-islam.5: Shia Islam can devalue through narratives of betrayal and unworthiness before the Imams.
shia-islam.6: Someone questions clerical authority and is told they are disrespecting the Ahl al-Bayt.
shia-islam.7: Questioning one's own clerical establishment is framed as betraying the Imams.
shia-islam.8: The annual mourning cycle delivers catharsis in seasons the institution conducts.
shia-islam.9: Love for the Ahl al-Bayt becomes mourning, majlis, clerical deference and suspicion.
shia-islam.10: Loyalty to the Ahl al-Bayt can mean love, mourning, deference or conformity.
shia-islam.11: Shia communities may accuse critics of betraying the oppressed while silencing the oppressed.
shia-islam.12: A person reports abuse by a cleric, and the response may deny it and accuse them of disrespect.
shia-islam.13: Repeated majlis, lamentation and chest beating can normalize intense states as loyalty.
shia-islam.14: Shia isolation can be built through sectarian identity, clerical networks and mourning cycles.
shia-islam.15: Shia triangulation often works through the Ahl al-Bayt, Karbala, marjaʿ authority and clerics.
shia-islam.16: A questioning person may be approached by family, organizers and clerics invoking Husayn.
shia-islam.17: Critics may be accused of disrespecting the Ahl al-Bayt, aiding enemies, or betraying Husayn.
shia-islam.18: A person questions clerical behavior and is told not to disrespect scholars.
shia-islam.19: A believer "chooses" clerical authority after being taught independent judgment is unsafe.
shia-islam.20: Shia spaces can bond through sacred grief: Karbala, martyrdom and the pain of betrayal.
shia-islam.21: A person who questions ritual intensity is met with grief, loyalty and accusations of betrayal.
shia-islam.22: Clerical authority and marjaʿ following may be framed as protection of the Ahl al-Bayt's path.
shia-islam.23: Marjaʿ following can become a structure where adult moral judgment is outsourced to clerics.
shia-islam.24: Shia identity can become organized around Karbala, mourning, loyalty and martyrdom.
shia-islam.26: Shia financial control may appear through khums and mosque and shrine donations.
shia-islam.27: Shia communities may manufacture crisis through narratives of enemies, betrayal and oppression.
shia-islam.28: A person questioning clerics or mourning culture may be treated as disloyal to the Ahl al-Bayt.
shia-islam.29: A person who questions ritual intensity is replaced by someone more visibly devoted.
shia-islam.30: A cleric may pressure loyalty through Karbala, then deny coercion: "It is only love."

sunni-islam.1: A convert is often quickly taught the "correct" prayer, creed, scholars and method.
sunni-islam.2: Sunni communities may provide mosque meals, Qur'an classes, rent help and convert mentorship.
sunni-islam.3: Sunni institutions often frame salvation around correct creed, prayer, practice and scholars.
sunni-islam.4: Someone leaving may be told to return to the Qur'an and Sunnah and speak to a proper scholar.
sunni-islam.5: Sunni environments can devalue by teaching the ordinary believer must rely on scholars.
sunni-islam.6: A believer asks about conflicting hadith and is told, "Ask people of knowledge."
sunni-islam.7: You must not interpret alone, and you must not choose among interpreters.
sunni-islam.8: Students get attention in unannounced portions, and competition for favor disciplines them.
sunni-islam.9: Following the Qur'an and Sunnah becomes the correct madhhab, aqidah and dress.
sunni-islam.10: "Follow the scholars" sounds clear, but which scholars count often shifts.
sunni-islam.11: Gatekeepers may accuse questioners of following desires while protecting their own authority.
sunni-islam.12: A person questions a scholar and hears, "You misunderstood the ruling" or "That is culture."
sunni-islam.13: Conservative Sunni environments can normalize constant correction of prayer, dress and speech.
sunni-islam.14: Sunni isolation can happen through approved-scholar ecosystems: avoid deviant sects.
sunni-islam.15: Sunni communities triangulate through scholars, madhhabs, fatwa sites, imams and parents.
sunni-islam.16: A questioning Muslim may be told by many to "ask a scholar," but only approved ones count.
sunni-islam.17: Sunni dissenters may be smeared as followers of desires, liberals, deviants, or arrogant.
sunni-islam.18: A believer is told to ask qualified scholars, but no answer may settle against the institution.
sunni-islam.19: A believer "chooses" a ruling after being told disagreement is following desires.
sunni-islam.20: Conservative Sunni environments may cycle correction and acceptance, then praise on alignment.
sunni-islam.21: Every unsatisfying answer leads to another scholar, another warning, another accusation.
sunni-islam.23: Laypeople may be told they cannot interpret texts or follow conscience without scholars.
sunni-islam.24: Sunni environments may define the person through correct aqidah, scholars, prayer and dress.
sunni-islam.25: Legal or gender harm may be bypassed with "Allah knows best" or "this is a test."
sunni-islam.26: Sunni communities may financially pressure members through fundraising and tuition.
sunni-islam.27: Conservative Sunni spaces may manufacture crisis through bidʿah panic and sectarian warnings.
sunni-islam.28: A believer who questions approved scholars may be labeled deviant, arrogant, or corrupted.
sunni-islam.30: Sunni institutions say "Follow qualified scholars," then define "qualified" as agreeing.

zoroastrianism.1: A member may be embraced through heritage, sacred fire and pride in an ancient tradition.
zoroastrianism.2: Zoroastrian communities may offer communal identity, sacred fire rituals and family networks.
zoroastrianism.3: Zoroastrianism offers cosmic vindication: good will overcome evil and creation will be renewed.
zoroastrianism.4: A Zoroastrian who distances may be pulled back by "We are so few" and "Preserve the fire."
zoroastrianism.5: Zoroastrianism can devalue through communal survival pressure, purity boundaries and ancestry.
zoroastrianism.6: Someone questions marriage restrictions and is told they are endangering an ancient faith.
zoroastrianism.7: In some communities, choosing to marry out is treated as choosing evil.
zoroastrianism.8: Young people feel alternating warmth and gatekeeping coolness keyed to marriage and observance.
zoroastrianism.9: Ritual participation expands into marriage boundaries, children's identity and funeral rites.
zoroastrianism.10: Community boundaries may be framed as theology, ancestry, survival or purity.
zoroastrianism.11: A small community may accuse someone who marries out of endangering the faith.
zoroastrianism.12: A person questions marriage restrictions; the response may deny coercion and cite preservation.
zoroastrianism.13: Survival pressure becomes normalized: marry within, preserve identity, protect rituals.
zoroastrianism.14: Zoroastrian isolation can occur through survival pressure and marriage expectations.
zoroastrianism.15: Zoroastrian triangulation can run through parents, priests, sacred fire and ancestry.
zoroastrianism.16: A Zoroastrian who marries out may face pressure from parents, priests and community elders.
zoroastrianism.17: A person who marries out may be smeared as selfish, careless, or weakening a small faith.
zoroastrianism.18: A person questioning marriage boundaries gets vague appeals to survival, purity and tradition.
zoroastrianism.19: A person "chooses" endogamy after being told the community is small and endangered.
zoroastrianism.20: A small community may create distress around survival: "We are few," "preserve the flame."
zoroastrianism.21: A person who tries to choose freely is met with survival anxiety.
zoroastrianism.22: Marriage expectations and ritual boundaries are framed as protecting an endangered faith.
zoroastrianism.23: Adults may be treated as irresponsible if they marry out or question ritual boundaries.
zoroastrianism.24: Identity may become tied to sacred fire, ancestry, purity, marriage and survival.
zoroastrianism.26: Zoroastrian financial control may involve fire temple support and ritual costs.
zoroastrianism.27: Zoroastrian communities may manufacture crisis around intermarriage and demographic decline.
zoroastrianism.28: A person who marries out may be treated as weakening the faith.
zoroastrianism.30: Endogamy is called personal choice, while marrying out marks someone as weakening a community.
